subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
subtitle: Balancing, Types of Reactions, Redox & Corrosion
summary: Master the law of conservation of mass in balanced chemical equations, five core reaction types (Combination, Decomposition, Displacement, Double Displacement, Redox), and everyday oxidation effects.

sections.title: Chemical Reactions & Balancing Equations
sections.summary: Observable chemical changes and mass conservation balancing.
paragraphs: A chemical reaction involves chemical change where original substances (reactants) lose their identity and form new substances (products) with entirely different properties.
Observable indicators of a chemical reaction include: change in state, change in colour, evolution of a gas, or change in temperature.

According to the Law of Conservation of Mass (Antoine Lavoisier), total mass of elements present in the products must equal the total mass of elements present in the reactants. Hence, every chemical equation must be balanced.

equations.notes: Iron reacts with steam (gaseous water) to produce magnetic iron oxide (iron(II,III) oxide) and hydrogen gas.
Magnesium ribbon is cleaned with sandpaper before burning to remove the protective layer of basic magnesium oxide/carbonate.

definitions.definition: A chemical equation in which the number of atoms of each element on the reactant side is equal to that on the product side, obeying the Law of Conservation of Mass.
keyPoints: Stoichiometric coefficients must be smallest whole integers

examTips.question: Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
examTips.answerOutline: Magnesium is a reactive metal. When stored, it reacts with atmospheric oxygen and moisture to form an unreactive coating of basic magnesium oxide (MgO). Sandpaper removes this coat so it burns smoothly.

keyTakeaways: Always use state symbols: solid (s), liquid (l), gas (g), aqueous solution (aq).
Catalysts, temperature, and pressure conditions are written above or below the reaction arrow.

sections.title: Types of Chemical Reactions
sections.summary: Combination, Decomposition, Displacement, and Double Displacement.
paragraphs: Chemical reactions can be classified into distinct patterns: Combination (two or more reactants combine into one single product), Decomposition (a single reactant splits into two or more products), Displacement (a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element), and Double Displacement (exchange of ions between two aqueous compounds forming a precipitate).

examTips.question: Why is the volume of gas collected in one of the test tubes during electrolysis of water double the volume in the other? Name this gas.
examTips.answerOutline: Water contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom per molecule (H₂O). On decomposition (2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂), hydrogen is liberated in double the molar volume of oxygen at the cathode.

keyTakeaways: Decomposition reactions require energy in the form of heat (thermal), light (photolytic), or electricity (electrolytic).
Silver chloride (AgCl) turns grey in sunlight: 2AgCl(s) → 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g), used in black and white photography.

subject: Biology
title: Life Processes
subtitle: Nutrition, Respiration, Transportation & Excretion
summary: A comprehensive synthesis of essential maintenance functions in living organisms: Autotrophic and Heterotrophic Nutrition, Respiration pathways, Double Circulation in the Human Heart, and Selective Reabsorption in the Nephron.

sections.title: What are Life Processes & Nutrition
sections.summary: Maintenance processes needed to prevent damage and break-down of body organs.
paragraphs: All living organisms perform life processes—maintenance operations that must continue even while an individual is asleep or inactive. Since energy is needed for these maintenance jobs, it must be taken from outside the body via nutrition.
In Autotrophic Nutrition, green plants take in carbon dioxide and water from the environment and convert them into stored carbohydrates (starch) using solar radiation trapped by chlorophyll.

Heterotrophs cannot synthesise organic molecules directly and depend upon autotrophs. Holozoic nutrition involves ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, and egestion, exemplified by Amoeba and human digestion.

definitions.definition: The fundamental biological functions performed by living organisms to maintain their existence, repair tissues, and sustain survival.
keyPoints: Energy is constantly required from external food sources

definitions.definition: A mode of nutrition where organisms synthesise their own food from simple inorganic raw materials like CO₂ and H₂O in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight.
keyPoints: Characteristic of green plants and cyanobacteria

equations.notes: Occurs in three steps: Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, conversion of light energy to chemical energy & splitting of water molecules, and reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates.

diagrams.title: Stomatal Apparatus (Open vs Closed Pore)
diagrams.caption: Guard cells swell when water flows into them, causing the stomatal pore to open. When guard cells lose water, they shrink and the pore closes.
diagrams.searchQuery: Stoma guard cells biology diagram

labels.name: Stomatal Pore
labels.description: Aperture for gas exchange (CO₂ and O₂)

examTips.question: How do desert plants take up carbon dioxide without losing excessive water?
examTips.answerOutline: Desert plants take up CO₂ at night when stomata are open and prepare an intermediate compound. During daylight, energy absorbed by chlorophyll acts on this intermediate.
examTips.commonPitfall: Students forget to mention night-time CO₂ uptake (crassulacean acid metabolism context).

keyTakeaways: Raw materials for photosynthesis: CO₂ (from air through stomata), H₂O (from soil via roots), sunlight, chlorophyll.
Bile juice does not contain enzymes but emulsifies large fat globules and provides an alkaline medium for pancreatic lipase.

sections.title: Respiration & Cellular Energy Breakdown
sections.summary: Glycolysis in cytoplasm followed by aerobic, anaerobic, or fermentation fates of pyruvate.
paragraphs: Respiration is the cellular process by which assimilated food is oxidised to release energy in the form of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), the energy currency of the cell.

The first step is Glycolysis: 1 molecule of 6-carbon Glucose is cleaved into two 3-carbon Pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm without requiring oxygen. The fate of pyruvate depends upon the availability of oxygen.

tables.title: Comparison: Aerobic vs Anaerobic Respiration
rows: Occurs in absence / deficiency of oxygen

equations.notes: Complete oxidation of pyruvate into carbon dioxide and water inside the mitochondrial matrix.
Accumulation of lactic acid in muscular tissue during intense physical exertion causes painful muscle cramps.

uncertainties.reason: Handwriting abbreviation in margin regarding first stage of pyruvate formation.
uncertainties.contextSnippet: Breakdown of glucose into pyruvate occurs in [Cytoplasm].

examTips.question: Why is the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms much faster than in terrestrial organisms?
examTips.answerOutline: The amount of dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared to the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere (~21%). Hence aquatic organisms must breathe at a faster rate to obtain sufficient oxygen.

keyTakeaways: ATP releases ~30.5 kJ/mol when terminal phosphate bond is broken by water.
Alveoli in lungs provide an enormous surface area (~80 m²) richly supplied with capillary networks for rapid gas diffusion.

sections.title: Transportation in Human Beings (Heart & Blood)
sections.summary: Double circulation mechanism, myogenic cardiac chambers, and blood vessel specialisations.
paragraphs: The human heart is a muscular organ as big as a clenched fist. Because both oxygen and carbon dioxide have to be transported by the blood, the heart has four distinct chambers to prevent oxygenated blood from mixing with deoxygenated blood.

Double circulation consists of two separate circuits: the Pulmonary Circuit (heart to lungs and back) and the Systemic Circuit (heart to rest of the body and back). This separation provides a highly efficient supply of oxygen needed to maintain constant warm-blooded body temperature.

diagrams.caption: Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from vena cava; right ventricle pumps it to lungs via pulmonary artery. Left atrium receives oxygenated blood from pulmonary veins; left ventricle pumps it to body via aorta.

examTips.question: Why is double circulation necessary in birds and mammals?
examTips.answerOutline: Warm-blooded animals (birds and mammals) constantly use energy to regulate their body temperature. Complete separation of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood provides the high metabolic efficiency needed.

keyTakeaways: Ventricles have much thicker muscular walls than atria because they have to pump blood out into various organs under high hydrostatic pressure.
Platelets circulate in blood and form clots at injury sites to prevent haemorrhage.

sections.title: Excretion in Human Beings (Nephron & Kidneys)
sections.summary: Ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, and tubular secretion in the nephron functional unit.
paragraphs: Excretion is the biological process by which harmful metabolic waste products (principally nitrogenous wastes like urea and uric acid produced in the liver) are eliminated from the body.

Each kidney contains approximately 1 to 1.2 million microscopic filtering units called Nephrons. Each nephron consists of a cup-shaped Bowman’s Capsule enclosing a tuft of capillaries called the Glomerulus, followed by a long coiled renal tubule (Proximal Convoluted Tubule, Henle’s Loop, Distal Convoluted Tubule, and Collecting Duct).
The initial glomerular filtrate (~180 litres per day in an adult) is largely reabsorbed along the tubular portion; only 1 to 2 litres is excreted daily as concentrated urine.

definitions.definition: The fundamental structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney that purifies blood, reabsorbs vital solutes, and concentrates urine.
keyPoints: Composed of Bowman’s capsule, glomerulus, Henle’s loop, collecting duct

definitions.definition: A clinical procedure for removing nitrogenous waste products from the blood of a patient suffering from renal failure using semi-permeable dialysing tubes immersed in dialysing fluid.
keyPoints: Dialysing fluid has same osmotic pressure as blood but lacks nitrogenous waste

diagrams.title: Structure of a Nephron (Renal Filtration Unit)
diagrams.caption: Ultrafiltration occurs in Bowman’s capsule under high pressure. Useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, water) are selectively reabsorbed in the coiled tubule.
diagrams.searchQuery: Nephron structure Bowman capsule loop of Henle diagram

labels.name: Glomerulus
labels.description: Capillary knot where ultrafiltration occurs under high pressure

labels.name: Henle’s Loop
labels.description: Hairpin loop reabsorbing water and sodium ions

labels.name: Collecting Duct
labels.description: Collects concentrated urine from multiple nephrons into ureter

examTips.question: Name four substances selectively reabsorbed from the initial filtrate as it passes through the nephron tubule.
examTips.answerOutline: 1. Glucose, 2. Amino acids, 3. Salts (NaCl), 4. Major amount of water (regulated by antidiuretic hormone and hydration state).

keyTakeaways: Ultrafiltration occurs because afferent arteriole is wider in diameter than the efferent arteriole, generating high hydrostatic pressure in glomerulus.
Plants excrete wastes differently: gaseous waste (O₂ and CO₂) via stomata, excess water via transpiration, dead cells shed via falling leaves, and resins/gums stored in old xylem.
